1.1: There was a man in the land of Uz called Job, and this man was an upright and just man, one that feared God, and eschewed evil.
1.2: And he had seue sonnes, and three daughters.
1.3: His substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels, and five hundreth yoke of oxen, and five hundreth she asses, and his family was very great, so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the East.
1.4: And his sonnes went and banketted in their houses, every one his day, and sent, and called their three sisters to eat and to drink with them.
1.5: And when the dayes of their banketting were gone about, Job sent, and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offred burnt offrings according to the nomber of them all. For Job thought, It may be that my sonnes have sinned, and blasphemed God in their hearts: thus did Job every day.
1.6: Now on a day when the children of God came and stood before the Lord, Satan came also among them.
1.7: Then the Lord sayde unto Satan, Whence comest thou? And Satan answered the Lord, saying, From compassing the earth to and from, and from walking in it.
1.8: And the Lord said unto Satan, Hast thou not considered my servant Job, how none is like him in the earth? an upright and just man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil?
1.9: Then Satan answered the Lord, and sayde, Doeth Job fear God for nought?
1.10: Hast thou not made an hedge about him and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side? thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land.
1.11: But stretch out now thine hand and touch all that he hath, to see if he will not blaspheme thee to thy face.
1.12: Then the Lord sayde unto Satan, Lo, all that he hath is in thine hand: onely upon himself shalt thou not stretch out thine hand. So Satan departed from the presence of the Lord.
1.13: And on a day, when his sonnes and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brothers house,
1.14: There came a messenger unto Job, and said, The oxen were plowing, and the asses feeding in their places,
1.15: And the Shabeans came violently, and took them: yea, they have slayne the servants with the edge of the sword: but I onely am escaped alone to tell thee.
1.16: And whiles he was yet speaking, another came, and sayde, The fire of God is fallen from the heaven, and hath burnt up the sheep and the servants, and deuoured them: but I onely am escaped alone to tell thee.
1.17: And whiles he was yet speaking, another came, and sayd, The Caldeans set on three bands, and fell upon the camels, and have taken them, and have slayne the seruantes with the edge of the sword: but I onely am escaped alone to tell thee.
1.18: And whiles he was yet speaking, came an other, and sayd, Thy sonnes, and thy daughters were eating, and drinking wine in their eldest brothers house,
1.19: And behold, there came a great wind from beyond the wilderness, and smote the four corners of the house, which fel upon the children, and they are dead, and I onely am escaped alone to tell thee.
1.20: Then Job arose, and rent his garment, and shaved his head, and fel down upon the ground, and worshipped,
1.21: And sayd, Naked came I out of my mothers womb, and naked shall I return thither: the Lord hath given, and the Lord hath taken it: blessed be the Name of the Lord.
1.22: In all this did not Job sinne, nor charge God foolishly.

2.1: And on a day the children of God came and stood before the Lord, and Satan came also among them, and stood before the Lord.
2.2: Then the Lord sayde unto Satan, Whence comest thou? And Satan answered the Lord, and sayd, From compassing the earth to and from, and from walking in it.
2.3: And the Lord sayd unto Satan, Hast thou not considered my servant Job, how none is like him in the earth? an upright and just man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil? for yet he continueth in his vprightnesse, although thou movedst me against him, to destroy him without cause.
2.4: And Satan answered the Lord, and sayde, Skin for skin, and all that ever a man hath, will he give for his life.
2.5: But stretch now out thine hand, and touch his bones and his flesh, to see if he will not blaspheme thee to thy face.
2.6: Then the Lord said unto Satan, Lo, he is in thine hand, but save his life.
2.7: So Satan departed from the presence of the Lord, and smote Job with sore boyles, from the sole of his foot unto his crown.
2.8: And he took a potsharde to scrape him, and he sat down among the ashes.
2.9: Then said his wife unto him, Doest thou continue yet in thine vprightnes? Blaspheme God, and dye.
2.10: But he said unto her, Thou speakest like a foolish woman: what? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and not receive evil? In all this did not Job sinne with his lippes.
2.11: Now when Iobs three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place, to wit, Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they were agreed together to come to lament with him, and to comfort him.
2.12: So when they lift up their eyes a far off, they knew him not: therefore they lift up their voyces and wept, and every one of them rent his garment, and sprinkled dust upon their heads toward the heaven.
2.13: So they sat by him upon the ground seven dayes, and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw, that the grief was very great.

3.1: Afterward Job opened his mouth, and cursed his day.
3.2: And Job cryed out, and sayd,
3.3: Let the day perish, wherein I was borne, and the night when it was sayde, There is a man child conceived.
3.4: Let that day bee darkenesse, let not God regard it from above, neyther let the light shine upon it,
3.5: But let darkenesse, and the shadow of death stain it: let the cloud remayne upon it, and let them make it fearefull as a bitter day.
3.6: Let darkenesse possess that night, let it not be ioyned unto the dayes of the yeere, nor let it come into the count of the moneths.
3.7: Yea, desolate be that night, and let no joy be in it.
3.8: Let them that curse the day, (being readie to renue their mourning) curse it.
3.9: Let the starres of that twilight be dimme through darkenesse of it: let it look for light, but have none: neither let it see the dawning of the day,
3.10: Because it shut not up the dores of my mothers womb: nor hid sorowe from mine eyes.
3.11: Why died I not in the birth? or why dyed I not, when I came out of the womb?
3.12: Why did the knees prevent me? and why did I suck the breasts?
3.13: For so should I now have lyen and been quiet, I should have slept then, and been at rest,
3.14: With the Kings and counselers of the earth, which have buylded themselves desolate places:
3.15: Or with the princes that had gold, and have filled their houses with silver.
3.16: Or why was I not hid, as an untimely birth, either as infants, which have not seen the light?
3.17: The wicked have there ceased from their tyrannie, and there they that laboured valiantly, are at rest.
3.18: The prisoners rest together, and hear not the voyce of the oppressour.
3.19: There are small and great, and the servant is free from his master.
3.20: Wherefore is the light given to him that is in miserie? and life unto them that have heauie hearts?
3.21: Which long for death, and if it come not, they would even search it more then treasures:
3.22: Which joy for gladnes, and reioyce, when they can find the grave.
3.23: Why is the light given to the man whose way is hid, and whom God hath hedged in?
3.24: For my sighing cometh before I eat, and my roarings are powred out like the water.
3.25: For the thing I feared, is come upon me, and the thing that I was afraid of, is come unto me.
3.26: I had no peace, neither had I quietness, neither had I rest, yet trouble is come.

4.1: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered, and sayde,
4.2: If we assay to commune with thee, wilt thou be grieved? but who can withhold himself from speaking?
4.3: Behold, thou hast taught many, and hast strengthened the wearie hands.
4.4: Thy wordes have confirmed him that was falling, and thou hast strengthened the weak knees.
4.5: But now it is come upon thee, and thou art grieved: it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled.
4.6: Is not this thy fear, thy confidence, thy pacience, and the vprightnesse of thy wayes?
4.7: Remember, I pray thee: who ever perished, being an innocent? or where were the upright destroyed?
4.8: As I have seen, they that plow iniquitie, and sow wickedness, reap the same.
4.9: With the blast of God they perish, and with the breath of his nostrels are they cosumed.
4.10: The roaring of the Lion, and the voyce of the Lioness, and the teeth of the Lions whelpes are broken.
4.11: The Lyon perisheth for lack of pray, and the Lyons whelpes are scattered abroad.
4.12: But a thing was brought to me secretly, and mine ear hath received a litle thereof.
4.13: In the thoughtes of ye visions of the night, when sleep falleth on men,
4.14: Fear came upon me, and dread which made all my bones to tremble.
4.15: And the wind passed before me, and made the heares of my flesh to stand up.
4.16: Then stood one, and I knew not his face: an image was before mine eyes, and in silence heard I a voyce, saying,
4.17: Shall man be more just then God? or shall a man be more pure then his maker?
4.18: Behold, he found no stedfastness in his Servants, and laid follie upon his Angels.
4.19: How much more in them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, which shalbe destroyed before the moth?
4.20: They be destroyed from the morning unto the evening: they perish for ever, without regard.
4.21: Doeth not their dignitie goe away with them? do they not die, and that without wisdom?

5.1: Call now, if any will answer thee, and to which of the Saintes wilt thou turn?
5.2: Doubtless anger killeth the foolish, and enuie slayeth the idiote.
5.3: I have seen the foolish well rooted, and suddenly I cursed his habitation, saying,
5.4: His children shalbe far from salvation, and they shall be destroyed in the gate, and none shall deliver them.
5.5: The hungrie shall eat up his harvest: yea, they shall take it from among the thornes, and the thirstie shall drink up their substance.
5.6: For miserie cometh not foorth of the dust, neither doeth affliction spring out of the earth.
5.7: But man is borne unto travail, as the sparkes flie vpwarde.
5.8: But I would inquire at God, and turn my talk unto God:
5.9: Which doeth great things and unsearchable, and marueilous things without nomber.
5.10: He giveth rain upon the earth, and powreth water upon the streetes,
5.11: And setteth up on hie them that be low, that the sorowfull may be exalted to salvation.
5.12: He scattereth the devices of the craftie: so that their handes can not accomplish that which they doe enterprise.
5.13: He taketh the wise in their craftiness, and the counsel of the wicked is made foolish.
5.14: They meet with darkenesse in the day time, and grope at noon day, as in the night.
5.15: But he saveth the poor from the sword, from their mouth, and from the hand of the violent man,
5.16: So that the poor hath his hope, but iniquitie shall stop her mouth.
5.17: Behold, blessed is the man whom God correcteth: therefore refuse not thou the chastising of the Almightie.
5.18: For he maketh the wound, and bindeth it up: he smiteth, and his handes make whole.
5.19: He shall deliver thee in six troubles, and in the seventh the evil shall not touch thee.
5.20: In famine he shall deliver thee from death: and in battel from the power of the sword.
5.21: Thou shalt be hid from the scourge of the tongue, and thou shalt not be afraid of destruction when it cometh.
5.22: But thou shalt laugh at destruction and dearth, and shalt not be afraid of the beast of the earth.
5.23: For the stones of the field shall be in league with thee, and the beastes of the field shall be at peace with thee.
5.24: And thou shalt know, that peace shall be in thy tabernacle, and thou shalt visit thine habitation, and shalt not sinne.
5.25: Thou shalt perceive also, that thy seed shalbe great, and thy posteritie as the grass of the earth.
5.26: Thou shalt goe to thy grave in a ful age, as a ricke of corn cometh in due season into the barn.
5.27: Lo, thus have we inquired of it, and so it is: hear this and know it for thy self.

6.2: Oh that my grief were well weighed, and my miseries were layed together in the balance.
6.3: For it would be now heavier then the sand of the sea: therefore my wordes are swallowed up.
6.4: For the arrowes of the Almightie are in me, the venime whereof doeth drink up my spirit, and the terrours of God fight against me.
6.5: Doeth the wild ass bray when he hath grass? or loweth the oxe when he hath fodder?
6.6: That which is vnsauerie, shall it be eaten without salt? or is there any taste in the white of an egg?
6.7: Such things as my soul refused to touch, as were sorowes, are my meat.
6.8: Oh that I might have my desire, and that God would grant me the thing that I long for!
6.9: That is, that God would destroy me: that he would let his hand go, and cut me off.
6.10: Then should I yet have comfort, (though I burn with sorowe, let him not spare) because I have not denyed the wordes of the Holy one.
6.11: What power have I that I should endure? or what is mine end, if I should prolong my life?
6.12: Is my strength the strength of stones? or is my flesh of brass?
6.13: Is it not so, that there is in me no help? and that strength is taken from me?
6.14: He that is in miserie, ought to be comforted of his neighbour: but men have forsaken the fear of the Almightie.
6.15: My brethre have deceived me as a brook, and as the rising of the rivers they pass away.
6.16: Which are blackish with yee, and wherein the snow is hid.
6.17: But in time they are dryed up with heat and are consumed: and when it is hot they fail out of their places,
6.18: Or they depart from their way and course, yea, they vanish and perish.
6.19: They that go to Tema, considered them, and they that goe to Sheba, waited for them.
6.20: But they were confounded: when they hoped, they came thither and were ashamed.
6.21: Surely now are ye like unto it: ye have seen my fearefull plague, and are afraid.
6.22: Was it because I said, Bring unto me? or give a reward to me of your substance?
6.23: And deliver me from the enemies hand, or ransom me out of the hand of tyrants?
6.24: Teach me, and I wil hold my tongue: and cause me to vnderstande, wherein I have erred.
6.25: How stedfast are the wordes of righteousnes? and what can any of you justly reprove?
6.26: Doe ye imagine to reprove wordes, that the talk of the afflicted should be as the wind?
6.27: Ye make your wrath to fall upon the fatherless, and dig a pit for your friend.
6.28: Now therefore be content to look upon me: for I will not lie before your face.
6.29: Turn, I pray you, let there be none iniquitie: return, I say, and ye shall see yet my righteousness in that behalf. Is there iniquitie in my tongue? doeth not my mouth feel sorowes?

7.1: Is there not an appointed time to man upon earth? and are not his dayes as the dayes of an hyreling?
7.2: As a servant longeth for the shadow, and as an hyreling looketh for the end of his work,
7.3: So have I had as an inheritance the moneths of vanitie, and painefull nights have been appointed unto me.
7.4: If I layed me down, I sayde, When shall I arise? and measuring the evening I am even full with tossing to and from unto the dawning of the day.
7.5: My flesh is clothed with wormes and filthiness of the dust: my skinne is rent, and become horrible.
7.6: My dayes are swifter then a weauers shittle, and they are spent without hope.
7.7: Remember that my life is but a wind, and that mine eye shall not return to see pleasure.
7.8: The eye that hath seen me, shall see me no more: thine eyes are upon me, and I shall be no longer.
7.9: As the cloud vanisheth and goeth away, so he that goeth down to the grave, shall come up no more.
7.10: He shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more.
7.11: Therefore I will not spare my mouth, but will speak in the trouble of my spirit, and muse in the bitterness of my mind.
7.12: Am I a sea or a whalefish, that thou keepest me in ward?
7.13: When I say, My couch shall relieve me, and my bed shall bring comfort in my meditation,
7.14: Then fearest thou me with dreames, and astonishest me with visions.
7.15: Therefore my soul chuseth rather to be strangled and to die, then to be in my bones.
7.16: I abhorre it, I shall not live alway: spare me then, for my dayes are but vanitie.
7.17: What is man, that thou doest magnifie him, and that thou settest thine heart upon him?
7.18: And doest visit him every morning, and tryest him every moment?
7.19: How long will it be yer thou depart from me? thou wilt not let me alone whiles I may swallow my spettle.
7.20: I have sinned, what shall I do unto thee? O thou preserver of me, why hast thou set me as a mark against thee, so that I am a burden unto my self?
7.21: And why doest thou not pardon my trespass? and take away mine iniquitie? for now shall I sleep in the dust, and if thou seekest me in the morning, I shall not be found.

8.1: Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said,
8.2: How long wilt thou talk of these things? and how long shall the wordes of thy mouth be as a mightie wind?
8.3: Doeth God pervert iudgement? or doeth the Almightie subuert justice?
8.4: If thy sonnes have sinned against him, and he hath sent them into the place of their iniquitie,
8.5: Yet if thou wilt early seek unto God, and pray to the Almightie,
8.6: If thou be pure and upright, then surely hee will awake up unto thee, and he wil make the habitation of thy righteousness prosperous.
8.7: And though thy beginning be small, yet thy latter end shall greatly encrease.
8.8: Inquire therefore, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thy self to search of their fathers.
8.9: (For we are but of yesterday, and are ignorant: for our dayes upon earth are but a shadow)
8.10: Shall not they teach thee and tell thee, and utter the wordes of their heart?
8.11: Can a rush grow without myre? or can ye grass grow without water?
8.12: Though it were in green and not cutte down, yet shall it wither before any other herb.
8.13: So are the paths of al that forget God, and the hypocrites hope shall perish.
8.14: His confidence also shalbe cut off, and his trust shalbe as the house of a spyder.
8.15: He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand: he shall hold him fast by it, yet shall it not endure.
8.16: The tree is green before the sunne, and the branches spread over the garden thereof.
8.17: The rootes thereof are wrapped about the fountain, and are folden about ye house of stones.
8.18: If any pluck it from his place, and it denie, saying, I have not seen thee,
8.19: Behold, it will reioyce by this meanes, that it may grow in another molde.
8.20: Behold, God will not cast away an upright man, neither will he take the wicked by the hand,
8.21: Till he have filled thy mouth with laughter, and thy lippes with joy.
8.22: They that hate thee, shall be clothed with shame, and the dwelling of the wicked shall not remain.

9.2: I know verily that it is so: for how should man compared unto God, be justified?
9.3: If I would dispute with him, hee could not answer him one thing of a thousand.
9.4: He is wise in heart, and mighty in strength: who hath been fierce against him and hath prospered?
9.5: He removeth the mountaines, and they feel not when he overthroweth them in his wrath.
9.6: Hee remooueth the earth out of her place, that the pillars thereof doe shake.
9.7: He commandeth the sunne, and it riseth not: hee closeth up the starres, as under a signet.
9.8: Hee himself alone spreadeth out the heavens, and walketh upon the height of the sea.
9.9: He maketh the starres Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the climates of the South.
9.10: He doeth great things, and vnsearcheable: yea, marueilous things without nomber.
9.11: Lo, when he goeth by me, I see him not: and when he passeth by, I perceive him not.
9.12: Behold, when he taketh a pray, who can make him to restore it? who shall say unto him, What doest thou?
9.13: God will not withdraw his anger, and the most mightie helpes doe stoupe under him.
9.14: How much less shall I answer him? or how should I find out my words with him?
9.15: For though I were just, yet could I not answer, but I would make supplication to my Judge.
9.16: If I cry, and he answer me, yet would I not beleeue, that he heard my voyce.
9.17: For he destroyeth mee with a tempest, and woundeth me without cause.
9.18: He wil not suffer me to take my breath, but filleth me with bitterness.
9.19: If we speak of strength, behold, he is strog: if we speak of iudgement, who shall bring me in to plead?
9.20: If I would iustifie my self, mine own mouth shall condemn mee: if I would be perfite, he shall judge me wicked.
9.21: Though I were perfite, yet I know not my soul: therefore abhorre I my life.
9.22: This is one point: therefore I said, Hee destroyeth the perfite and the wicked.
9.23: If the scourge should suddenly slay, should God laugh at the punishment of the innocent?
9.24: The earth is given into the hand of ye wicked: he covereth the faces of the judges therof: if not, where is he? or who is he?
9.25: My dayes have been more swift then a post: they have fled, and have seen no good thing.
9.26: They are passed as with the most swift ships, and as the eagle that flyeth to the pray.
9.27: If I say, I wil forget my complaynt, I will cease from my wrath, and comfort mee,
9.28: Then I am afrayd of all my sorowes, knowing that thou wilt not judge me innocent.
9.29: If I be wicked, why labour I thus in vain?
9.30: If I wash my self with snow water, and purge mine hands most clean,
9.31: Yet shalt thou plunge mee in the pit, and mine own clothes shall make me filthie.
9.32: For he is not a man as I am, that I should answer him, if we come together to iudgement.
9.33: Neyther is there any vmpire that might lay his hand upon us both.
9.34: Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear astonish me:
9.35: Then will I speak, and fear him not: but because I am not so, I hold me still.

10.1: My soul is cut off though I live: I wil leave my complaint upon my self, and wil speak in the bitterness of my soul.
10.2: I will say unto God, Condemn mee not: shew me, wherefore thou contendest with mee.
10.3: Thinkest thou it good to oppress me, and to cast off the labour of thine handes, and to fauour the counsel of the wicked?
10.4: Hast thou carnal eyes? or doest thou see as man seeth?
10.5: Are thy dayes as mans dayes? or thy yeres, as the time of man,
10.6: That thou inquirest of mine iniquitie, and searchest out my sinne?
10.7: Thou knowest that I can not do wickedly: for none can deliver me out of thine hand.
10.8: Thine handes have made me, and fashioned mee wholy round about, and wilt thou destroy me?
10.9: Remember, I pray thee, that thou hast made me as the clay, and wilt thou bring me into dust again?
10.10: Hast thou not powred me out as milk? and turned me to cruds like cheese?
10.11: Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and ioyned me together with bones and sinewes.
10.12: Thou hast given me life, and grace: and thy visitation hath preserved my spirit.
10.13: Though thou hast hid these things in thine heart, yet I know that it is so with thee.
10.14: If I have sinned, then thou wilt streightly look unto me, and wilt not hold mee giltlesse of mine iniquitie.
10.15: If I have done wickedly, wo unto me: if I have done righteously, I will not lift up mine head, being full of confusion, because I see mine affliction.
10.16: But let it increase: hunt thou me as a lyon: return and shew thy self marueilous upon me.
10.17: Thou renuest thy plagues against me, and thou increasest thy wrath against me: changes and armies of sorowes are against me.
10.18: Wherfore then hast thou brought me out of the womb? Oh that I had perished, and that none eye had seen me!
10.19: And that I were as I had not been, but brought from the womb to the grave!
10.20: Are not my dayes few? let him cease, and leave off from me, that I may take a litle comfort,
10.21: Before I goe and shall not return, even to the land of darkenesse and shadow of death:
10.22: Into a land, I say, dark as darknes it self, and into the shadow of death, where is none order, but the light is there as darkenesse.

11.1: Then answered Zophar the Naamathite, and sayde,
11.2: Should not the multitude of wordes be answered? or should a great talker be justified?
11.3: Should men hold their peace at thy lyes? and when thou mockest others, shall none make thee ashamed?
11.4: For thou hast sayde, My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in thine eyes.
11.5: But, oh that God would speak and open his lippes against thee!
11.6: That he might shew thee the secretes of wisedome, how thou hast deserued double, according to right: know therefore that God hath forgotten thee for thine iniquitie.
11.7: Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out ye Almighty to his perfection?
11.8: The heavens are hie, what canst thou doe? it is deeper then the hell, how canst thou know it?
11.9: The measure thereof is longer then the earth, and it is broader then the sea.
11.10: If hee cut off and shut up, or gather together, who can turn him back?
11.11: For hee knoweth vain men, and seeth iniquitie, and him that understandeth nothing.
11.12: Yet vain man would be wise, though man new borne is like a wild ass colt.
11.13: If thou prepare thine heart, and stretch out thine hands toward him:
11.14: If iniquitie be in thine hand, put it far away, and let no wickedness dwell in thy Tabernacle.
11.15: The truely shalt thou lift up thy face without spot, and shalt be stable, and shalt not fear.
11.16: But thou shalt forget thy miserie, and remember it as waters that are past.
11.17: Thine age also shall appear more clear then the noon day: thou shalt shine and bee as the morning.
11.18: And thou shalt bee bold, because there is hope: and thou shalt digge pittes, and shalt lye down safely.
11.19: For when thou takest thy rest, none shall make thee afraid: yea, many shall make sute unto thee.
11.20: But the eyes of the wicked shall fail, and their refuge shall perish, and their hope shalbe sorow of mind.

12.2: In deed because that ye are the people onely, wisedome must dye with you.
12.3: But I have understanding aswel as you, and am not inferior unto you: yea, who knoweth not such things?
12.4: I am as one mocked of his neighbour, who calleth upon God, and he heareth him: the just and the upright is laughed to scorn.
12.5: Hee that is readie to fall, is as a lamp despised in the opinion of the rich.
12.6: The tabernacles of robbers doe prosper, and they are in safetie, that provoke God, whom God hath enriched with his hand.
12.7: Ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee, and the foules of the heaven, and they shall tell thee:
12.8: Or speak to the earth, and it shall shew thee: or the fishes of the sea, and they shall declare unto thee.
12.9: Who is ignorant of all these, but that the hand of the Lord hath made these?
12.10: In whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind.
12.11: Doeth not the eares discern the words? and the mouth taste meat for it self?
12.12: Among the ancient is wisedome, and in the length of dayes is understanding.
12.13: With him is wisedome and strength: he hath counsel and understanding.
12.14: Behold, he will break down, and it can not be built: he shutteth a man up, and he can not be loosed.
12.15: Behold, he withholdeth the waters, and they drie up: but when he sendeth them out, they destroy the earth.
12.16: With him is strength and wisedome: hee that is deceived, and that deceiveth, are his.
12.17: He causeth the counsellers to goe as spoyled, and maketh the judges fooles.
12.18: He looseth the collar of Kings, and girdeth their loynes with a girdle.
12.19: He leadeth away the princes as a pray, and overthroweth the mightie.
12.20: He taketh away the speach from the faithful counsellers, and taketh away the iudgement of the ancient.
12.21: He powreth contempt upon princes, and maketh the strength of the mightie weak.
12.22: He discovereth the deep places from their darkenesse, and bringeth foorth the shadow of death to light.
12.23: He increaseth the people, and destroyeth them: he inlargeth the nations, and bringeth them in again.
12.24: He taketh away the heartes of the that are the chief over the people of the earth, and maketh them to wander in the wildernes out of the way.
12.25: They grope in the dark without light: and he maketh the to stagger like a drunken man.

13.1: Loe, mine eye hath seen all this: mine ear hath heard, and vnderstande it.
13.2: I know also as much as you know: I am not inferiour unto you.
13.3: But I will speak to the Almightie, and I desire to dispute with God.
13.4: For in deed ye forge lyes, and all you are physitions of no value.
13.5: Oh, that you would hold your tongue, that it might be imputed to you for wisedome!
13.6: Now hear my disputation, and give ear to the arguments of my lips.
13.7: Will ye speak wickedly for Gods defence, and talk deceitfully for his cause?
13.8: Will ye accept his person? or will ye contend for God?
13.9: Is it well that he should seek of you? will you make a lye for him, as one lyeth for a man?
13.10: He will surely reprooue you, if ye doe secretly accept any person.
13.11: Shall not his excellencie make you afraid? and his fear fall upon you?
13.12: Your memories may be compared unto ashes, and your bodyes to bodyes of clay.
13.13: Hold your tongues in my presence, that I may speak, and let come upon what will.
13.14: Wherefore doe I take my flesh in my teeth, and put my soul in mine hand?
13.15: Loe, though he slay me, yet will I trust in him, and I will reprooue my wayes in his sight.
13.16: He shalbe my salvation also: for the hypocrite shall not come before him.
13.17: Hear diligently my wordes, and mark my talk.
13.18: Behold now: if I prepare me to iudgement, I know that I shalbe justified.
13.19: Who is he, that will plead with me? for if I now hold my tongue, I dye.
13.20: But doe not these two things unto me: then will I not hide my self from thee.
13.21: Withdraw thine hand from me, and let not thy fear make me afraid.
13.22: Then call thou, and I will answer: or let me speak, and answer thou me.
13.23: How many are mine iniquities and sinnes? shew me my rebellion, and my sinne.
13.24: Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and takest me for thine enemie?
13.25: Wilt thou break a leaf driven to and from? and wilt thou pursue the drie stubble?
13.26: For thou writest bitter things against me, and makest me to possess the iniquities of my youth.
13.27: Thou puttest my feet also in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my pathes, and makest the print thereof in ye heeles of my feet.
13.28: Such one consumeth like a rotten thing, and as a garment that is motheaten.

14.1: Man that is borne of woman, is of short continuance, and full of trouble.
14.2: He shooteth foorth as a flowre, and is cut down: he vanisheth also as a shadow, and continueth not.
14.3: And yet thou openest thine eyes upon such one, and causest me to enter into iudgement with thee.
14.4: Who can bring a clean thing out of filthiness? there is not one.
14.5: Are not his dayes determined? the nober of his moneths are with thee: thou hast appointed his boundes, which he can not pass.
14.6: Turn from him that he may cease until his desired day, as an hyreling.
14.7: For there is hope of a tree, if it bee cut down, that it will yet sprout, and the branches thereof will not cease.
14.8: Though the root of it wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof be dead in ye ground,
14.9: Yet by the sent of water it will bud, and bring foorth boughes like a plant.
14.10: But man is sick, and dyeth, and man perisheth, and where is he?
14.11: As the waters pass from the sea, and as the flood decayeth and dryeth up,
14.12: So man sleepeth and riseth not: for hee shall not wake again, nor be raised from his sleep till the heaven be no more.
14.13: Oh that thou wouldest hide me in the grave, and keep me secret, until thy wrath were past, and wouldest give me terme, and remember me.
14.14: If a man die, shall he live again? All the dayes of mine appointed time will I wait, till my changing shall come.
14.15: Thou shalt call me, and I shall answer thee: thou lovest the work of thine own hands.
14.16: But now thou nombrest my steppes, and doest not delay my sinnes.
14.17: Mine iniquitie is sealed up, as in a bagge, and thou addest unto my wickedness.
14.18: And surely as the mountain that falleth, cometh to nought, and the rock that is remooued from his place:
14.19: As the water breaketh the stones, when thou ouerflowest the things which grow in the dust of ye earth: so thou destroyest ye hope of man.
14.20: Thou prevailest alway against him, so that he passeth away: he changeth his face when thou castest him away.
14.21: And he knoweth not if his sonnes shall be honourable, neither shall he understand concerning them, whether they shalbe of low degree,
14.22: But while his flesh is upon him, he shall be sorowfull, and while his soul is in him, it shall mourn.

15.1: Then answered Eliphaz the Temanite, and said,
15.2: Shal a wise man speak words of ye wind, and fill his bellie with the East wind?
15.3: Shall he dispute with wordes not comely? or with talk that is not profitable?
15.4: Surely thou hast cast off fear, and restrainest prayer before God.
15.5: For thy mouth declareth thine iniquitie, seeing thou hast chosen ye tongue of the crafty.
15.6: Thine own mouth condemneth thee, and not I, and thy lippes testifie against thee.
15.7: Art thou the first man, that was borne? and wast thou made before the hils?
15.8: Hast thou heard the secret counsel of God, and doest thou restrain wisedome to thee?
15.9: What knowest thou that we know not? and understandest that is not in us?
15.10: With us are both auncient and very aged men, far older then thy father.
15.11: Seem the consolations of God small unto thee? is this thing strange unto thee?
15.12: Why doeth thine heart take thee away, and what doe thine eyes mean,
15.13: That thou answerest to God at thy pleasure, and bringest such wordes out of thy mouth?
15.14: What is man, that he should be clean? and he that is borne of woman, that he should be just?
15.15: Behold, he found no stedfastness in his Saintes: yea, the heavens are not clean in his sight.
15.16: How much more is man abominable, and filthie, which drinketh iniquitie like water?
15.17: I will tell thee: hear me, and I will declare that which I have seen:
15.18: Which wise men have told, as they have heard of their fathers, and have not kept it secret:
15.19: To whom alone the land was given and no stranger passed through them.
15.20: The wicked man is continually as one that traueileth of child, and the nomber of yeeres is hid from the tyrant.
15.21: A sound of fear is in his eares, and in his prosperitie the destroyer shall come upon him.
15.22: He beleeueth not to return out of darkness: for he seeth the sword before him.
15.23: He wandreth to and from for bread where he may: he knoweth that the day of darkenesse is prepared at hand.
15.24: Affliction and anguish shall make him afraid: they shall prevail against him as a King readie to the battell.
15.25: For he hath stretched out his hand against GOD, and made him self strong against the Almightie.
15.26: Therefore God shall runne upon him, even upon his neck, and against the most thick part of his shield.
15.27: Because he hath covered his face with his fatness, and hath colloppes in his flancke.
15.28: Though he dwell in desolate cities, and in houses which no man inhabiteth, but are become heapes,
15.29: He shall not be rich, neither shall his substance continue, neither shall he prolong the perfection thereof in the earth.
15.30: He shall never depart out of darkenesse: the flame shall drie up his branches, and he shall goe away with the breath of his mouth.
15.31: He beleeueth not that he erreth in vanitie: therefore vanitie shalbe his change.
15.32: His branch shall not be green, but shall be cut off before his day.
15.33: God shall destroy him as the vine her sower grape, and shall cast him off, as the olive doeth her flowre.
15.34: For the congregation of the hypocrite shalbe desolate, and fire shall deuoure the houses of bribes.
15.35: For they conceive mischief and bring foorth vanitie, and their bellie hath prepared deceit.

16.2: I have oft times heard such things: miserable comforters are ye all.
16.3: Shall there be none end of wordes of wind? or what maketh thee bold so to answer?
16.4: I could also speak as yee doe: (but would God your soul were in my soules stead) I could keep you company in speaking, and could shake mine head at you,
16.5: But I would strengthen you with my mouth, and the comfort of my lips should asswage your sorowe.
16.6: Though I speak, my sorow can not be asswaged: though I cease, what release have I?
16.7: But now hee maketh mee wearie: O God, thou hast made all my congregation desolate,
16.8: And hast made me full of wrinkles which is a witness thereof, and my leannes ryseth up in me, testifying the same in my face.
16.9: His wrath hath torn me, and hee hateth me, and gnasheth upon mee with his teeth: mine enemie hath sharpened his eyes against me.
16.10: They have opened their mouthes upon me, and smitten me on the cheek in reproch; they gather themselves together against me.
16.11: God hath delivered me to the vniust, and hath made mee to turn out of the way by the hands of the wicked.
16.12: I was in welth, but he hath brought me to nought: he hath taken me by the neck, and beaten me, and set me as a mark for himself.
16.13: His archers compass mee round about: he cutteth my reines, and doth not spare, and powreth my gall upon the ground.
16.14: He hath broken me with one breaking upon another, and runneth upon me like a gyant.
16.15: I have sowed a sackcloth upon my skinne, and have abased mine horn unto the dust.
16.16: My face is withered with weeping, and the shadow of death is upon mine eyes,
16.17: Though there be no wickedness in mine hands, and my prayer be pure.
16.18: O earth, cover not thou my blood, and let my crying find no place.
16.19: For lo, now my witness is in the heaven, and my record is on hie.
16.20: My friends speak eloquently against me: but mine eye powreth out teares unto God.
16.21: Oh that a man might plead with God, as man with his neighbour!
16.22: For the yeeres accounted come, and I shall go the way, whence I shall not return.

17.1: My breath is corrupt: my dayes are cut off, and the grave is readie for me.
17.2: There are none but mockers with mee, and mine eye continueth in their bitterness.
17.3: Lay down now and put me in suretie for thee: who is hee, that will touch mine hand?
17.4: For thou hast hid their heart from understanding: therefore shalt thou not set them up on hie.
17.5: For the eyes of his children shall fail, that speaketh flattery to his friends.
17.6: Hee hath also made mee a byword of the people, and I am as a Tabret before them.
17.7: Mine eye therefore is dimme for grief, and all my strength is like a shadow.
17.8: The righteous shalbe astonied at this, and the innocent shalbe moved against ye hypocrite.
17.9: But the righteous wil hold his way, and he whose hands are pure, shall increase his strength.
17.10: All you therefore turn you, and come now, and I shall not find one wise among you.
17.11: My dayes are past, mine enterprises are broken, and the thoughts of mine heart
17.12: Have changed the nyght for the day, and the light that approched, for darkenesse.
17.13: Though I hope, yet the grave shall bee mine house, and I shall make my bed in the dark.
17.14: I shall say to corruption, Thou art my father, and to the worm, Thou art my mother and my sister.
17.15: Where is then now mine hope? or who shall consider the thing, that I hoped for?
17.16: They shall goe down into the bottom of the pit: surely it shall lye together in the dust.

18.1: Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said,
18.2: When will yee make an end of your words? cause us to vnderstande, and then wee will speak.
18.3: Wherefore are wee counted as beastes, and are vile in your sight?
18.4: Thou art as one that teareth his soul in his anger. Shall the earth bee forsaken for thy sake? or the rock removed out of his place?
18.5: Yea, the light of the wicked shalbe quenched, and the spark of his fire shall not shine.
18.6: The light shalbe dark in his dwelling, and his candle shalbe put out with him.
18.7: The steps of his strength shalbe restrained, and his own counsel shall cast him down.
18.8: For hee is taken in the net by his feet, and he walketh upon the snares.
18.9: The grenne shall take him by the heel, and the theefe shall come upon him.
18.10: A snare is layed for him in the ground, and a trappe for him in the way.
18.11: Fearefulnesse shall make him afrayde on every side, and shall drive him to his feet.
18.12: His strength shalbe famine: and destruction shalbe readie at his side.
18.13: It shall deuoure the inner partes of his skinne, and the first borne of death shall deuoure his strength.
18.14: His hope shalbe rooted out of his dwelling, and shall cause him to go to the King of fear.
18.15: Fear shall dwell in his house (because it is not his) and brimstone shalbe scattered upon his habitation.
18.16: His rootes shalbe dryed up beneath, and above shall his branch be cut down.
18.17: His remembrance shall perish from the earth, and he shall have no name in the street.
18.18: They shall drive him out of the light unto darkenesse, and chase him out of the world.
18.19: Hee shall neither have sonne nor nephew among his people, nor any posteritie in his dwellings.
18.20: The posteritie shalbe astonied at his day, and fear shall come upon the ancient.
18.21: Surely such are the habitations of the wicked, and this is the place of him that knoweth not God.

19.2: How long will yee vex my soul, and torment me with wordes?
19.3: Ye have now ten times reproched me, and are not ashamed: ye are impudent toward mee.
19.4: And though I had in deed erred, mine errour remaineth with me.
19.5: But in deed if ye will aduance your selves against me, and rebuke me for my reproche,
19.6: Know now, that God hath ouerthrowen me, and hath compassed me with his net.
19.7: Behold, I crie out of violence, but I have none answer: I crie, but there is no iudgement.
19.8: Hee hath hedged up my way that I cannot pass, and he hath set darkenesse in my paths.
19.9: Hee hath spoyled mee of mine honour, and taken the crown away from mine head.
19.10: He hath destroyed mee on every side and I am gone: and he hath removed mine hope like a tree.
19.11: And he hath kindled his wrath against me, and counteth mee as one of his enemies.
19.12: His armies came together, and made their way upon me, and camped about my tabernacle.
19.13: He hath remooued my brethre far from me, and also mine acquaintance were strangers unto me.
19.14: My neighbours have forsaken me, and my familiars have forgotten me.
19.15: They that dwel in mine house, and my maydes took me for a stranger: for I was a stranger in their sight.
19.16: I called my servant, but he would not answer, though I prayed him with my mouth.
19.17: My breath was strange unto my wife, though I prayed her for the childrens sake of mine own body.
19.18: The wicked also despised mee, and when I rose, they spake against me.
19.19: All my secret friends abhorred me, and they whom I loved, are turned against me.
19.20: My bone cleaveth to my skinne and to my flesh, and I have escaped with the skinne of my teeth.
19.21: Have pitie upon me: have pitie upon me, (O yee my friendes) for the hand of God hath touched me.
19.22: Why do ye persecute me, as God? and are not satisfied with my flesh?
19.23: Oh that my wordes were now written! oh that they were written even in a book,
19.24: And graven with an yron pen in lead, or in stone for ever!
19.25: For I am sure, that my Redeemer liveth, and he shall stand the last on the earth.
19.26: And though after my skin wormes destroy this bodie, yet shall I see God in my flesh.
19.27: Whom I my self shall see, and mine eyes shall behold, and none other for me, though my reynes are consumed within me.
19.28: But yee sayde, Why is hee persecuted? And there was a deep matter in me.
19.29: Be ye afraid of the sword: for the sword will be avenged of wickedness, that yee may know that there is a iudgement.

20.1: Then answered Zophar the Naamathite and said,
20.2: Doubtless my thoughts cause me to answer, and therefore I make haste.
20.3: I have heard the correction of my reproch: therefore the spirit of mine understanding causeth me to answer.
20.4: Knowest thou not this of old? and since God placed man upon the earth,
20.5: That the reioycing of the wicked is short, and that the joy of hypocrites is but a moment?
20.6: Though his excellencie mount up to the heaven, and his head reach unto the cloudes,
20.7: Yet shall hee perish for ever, like his dung, and they which have seen him, shall say, Where is hee?
20.8: He shall flee away as a dream, and they shall not find him, and shall pass away as a vision of the night,
20.9: So that the eye which had seen him, shall do so no more, and his place shall see him no more.
20.10: His children shall flatter the poor, and his hands shall restore his substance.
20.11: His bones are full of the sinne of his youth, and it shall lie down with him in the dust.
20.12: When wickedness was sweet in his mouth, and he hid it under his tongue,
20.13: And fauoured it, and would not forsake it, but kept it close in his mouth,
20.14: Then his meat in his bowels was turned: the gall of Aspes was in the middes of him.
20.15: He hath deuoured substance, and hee shall vomit it: for God shall draw it out of his bellie.
20.16: He shall suck the gall of Aspes, and the vipers tongue shall slay him.
20.17: He shall not see the rivers, nor the floods and streames of honie and butter.
20.18: He shall restore the labour, and shall deuoure no more: even according to the substance shalbe his exchange, and he shall enioy it no more.
20.19: For he hath undone many: he hath forsaken the poor, and hath spoyled houses which he builded not.
20.20: Surely he shall feel no quietnes in his bodie, neither shall he reserve of that which he desired.
20.21: There shall none of his meat bee left: therefore none shall hope for his goods.
20.22: When he shalbe filled with his abundance, he shalbe in pain, and the hand of all the wicked shall assaile him.
20.23: He shall be about to fill his belly, but God shall send upon him his fierce wrath, and shall cause to rayne upon him, even upon his meat.
20.24: He shall flee from the yron weapons, and the bow of steel shall strike him through.
20.25: The arrow is drawen out, and cometh forth of the body, and shineth of his gall, so fear cometh upon him.
20.26: All darkenes shalbe hid in his secret places: the fire that is not blowen, shall deuoure him, and that which remaineth in his tabernacle, shalbe destroyed.
20.27: The heaven shall declare his wickednes, and the earth shall rise up against him.
20.28: The increase of his house shall go away: it shall flow away in the day of his wrath.
20.29: This is the portion of the wicked man from God, and the heritage that he shall have of God for his wordes.

21.2: Hear diligently my wordes, and this shalbe in stead of your consolations.
21.3: Suffer mee, that I may speak, and when I have spoken, mock on.
21.4: Doe I direct my talk to man? If it were so, how should not my spirit be troubled?
21.5: Mark mee, and be abashed, and lay your hand upon your mouth.
21.6: Even when I remember, I am afrayde, and fear taketh hold on my flesh.
21.7: Wherefore do the wicked live, and wax old, and grow in wealth?
21.8: Their seed is established in their sight with them, and their generation before their eyes.
21.9: Their houses are peaceable without fear, and the rod of God is not upon them.
21.10: Their bullock gendreth, and fayleth not: their cow calveth, and casteth not her calf.
21.11: They send forth their children like sheep, and their sonnes dance.
21.12: They take the tabret and harp, and reioyce in the sound of the organs.
21.13: They spend their dayes in wealth, and suddenly they go down to the grave.
21.14: They say also unto God, Depart from us: for we desire not the knowledge of thy wayes.
21.15: Who is the Almightie, that we should serve him? and what profit should we have, if we should pray unto him?
21.16: Lo, their wealth is not in their hand: therfore let the counsel of the wicked bee far from me.
21.17: How oft shall the candle of the wicked be put out? and their destruction come upon them? he wil deuide their lives in his wrath.
21.18: They shall be as stubble before the wind, and as chaff that the storm carieth away.
21.19: God wil lay up the sorowe of the father for his children: when he rewardeth him, hee shall know it.
21.20: His eyes shall see his destruction, and he shall drink of the wrath of the Almightie.
21.21: For what pleasure hath he in his house after him, when the nomber of his moneths is cut off?
21.22: Shall any teach God knowledge, who judgeth the highest things?
21.23: One dyeth in his full strength, being in all ease and prosperitie.
21.24: His breasts are full of milk, and his bones runne full of marowe.
21.25: And another dieth in the bitternes of his soul, and never eateth with pleasure.
21.26: They shall sleep both in the dust, and the wormes shall cover them.
21.27: Behold, I know your thoughts, and the enterprises, wherewith ye do me wrong.
21.28: For ye say, Where is the princes house? and where is the tabernacle of the wickeds dwelling?
21.29: May ye not ask the that go by the way? and ye can not deny their signes.
21.30: But the wicked is kept unto the day of destruction, and they shall be brought forth to the day of wrath.
21.31: Who shall declare his way to his face? and who shall reward him for that he hath done?
21.32: Yet shall he be brought to the grave, and remain in the heap.
21.33: The slimie valley shalbe sweet unto him, and every man shall draw after him, as before him there were innumerable.
21.34: How then comfort ye me in vain, seeing in your answeres there remain but lyes?

22.1: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered, and sayde,
22.2: May a man be profitable unto God, as he that is wise, may be profitable to himself?
22.3: Is it any thing unto the Almightie, that thou art righteous? or is it profitable to him, that thou makest thy wayes upright?
22.4: Is it for fear of thee that he will accuse thee? or go with thee into iudgement?
22.5: Is not thy wickednes great, and thine iniquities innumerable?
22.6: For thou hast taken the pledge from thy brother for nought, and spoyled the clothes of the naked.
22.7: To such as were wearie, thou hast not given water to drink, and hast withdrawen bread from the hungrie.
22.8: But the mightie man had the earth, and he that was in autoritie, dwelt in it.
22.9: Thou hast cast out widowes emptie, and the armes of the fatherles were broken.
22.10: Therefore snares are round about thee, and fear shall suddenly trouble thee:
22.11: Or darkenes that thou shouldest not see, and abundance of waters shall cover thee.
22.12: Is not God on hie in the heaven? and behold the height of the starres how hie they are.
22.13: But thou sayest, How should God know? can he judge through the dark cloud?
22.14: The cloudes hide him that he can not see, and he walketh in the circle of heaven.
22.15: Hast thou marked the way of the world, wherein wicked men have walked?
22.16: Which were cut down before the time, whose foundation was as a river that overflowed:
22.17: Which sayd unto God, Depart from us, and asked what the Almightie could do for them.
22.18: Yet hee filled their houses with good things: but let the counsel of the wicked be far from me.
22.19: The righteous shall see them, and shall reioyce, and the innocent shall laugh them to scorn.
22.20: Surely our substance is hid: but the fire hath deuoured the remnant of them.
22.21: Therefore acquaint thy self, I pray thee, with him, and make peace: thereby thou shalt have prosperitie.
22.22: Receive, I pray thee, the law of his mouth, and lay up his words in thine heart.
22.23: If thou return to the Almightie, thou shalt be buylt up, and thou shalt put iniquitie far from thy tabernacle.
22.24: Thou shalt lay up gold for dust, and the gold of Ophir, as the flintes of the rivers.
22.25: Yea, the Almightie shalbe thy defence, and thou shalt have plentie of silver.
22.26: And thou shalt then delite in the Almightie, and lift up thy face unto God.
22.27: Thou shalt make thy praier unto him, and he shall hear thee, and thou shalt render thy vowes.
22.28: Thou shalt also decree a thing, and he shall establish it unto thee, and the light shall shine upon thy wayes.
22.29: When others are cast down, then shalt thou say, I am lifted up: and God shall save the humble person.
22.30: The innocent shall deliver the yland, and it shalbe preserved by the purenes of thine hands.

23.2: Though my talk be this day in bitternes, and my plague greater then my groning,
23.3: Would God yet I knew how to find him, I would enter unto his place.
23.4: I would plead the cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments.
23.5: I would know the wordes, that he would answer me, and would understand what he would say unto me.
23.6: Would he plead against me with his great power? No, but he would put strength in me.
23.7: There the righteous might reason with him, so I should be delivered for ever from my Judge.
23.8: Behold, if I go to the East, he is not there: if to the West, yet I can not perceive him:
23.9: If to the North where he worketh, yet I cannot see him: he wil hide himself in the South, and I cannot behold him.
23.10: But he knoweth my way, and trieth mee, and I shall come forth like the gold.
23.11: My foot hath followed his steps: his way have I kept, and have not declined.
23.12: Neyther have I departed from the commandement of his lippes, and I have esteemed the words of his mouth more then mine appointed food.
23.13: Yet he is in one mind, and who can turn him? yea, he doeth what his mind desireth.
23.14: For he will perform that, which is decreed of me, and many such things are with him.
23.15: Therefore I am troubled at his presence, and in considering it, I am afraid of him.
23.16: For God hath softened mine heart, and the Almightie hath troubled me.
23.17: For I am not cut off in darkness, but he hath hid the darkenesse from my face.

24.1: How should not the times be hid from the Almightie, seeing that they which know him, see not his dayes?
24.2: Some remove the land marks, that rob the flockes and feed thereof.
24.3: They lead away the ass of the fatherles: and take the widowes oxe to pledge.
24.4: They make the poor to turn out of the way, so that the poor of the earth hide themselves together.
24.5: Behold, others as wild asses in the wilderness, goe forth to their business, and rise early for a pray: the wilderness giveth him and his children food.
24.6: They reap his provision in the field, but they gather the late vintage of the wicked.
24.7: They cause the naked to lodge without garment, and without covering in the cold.
24.8: They are wet with the showres of the moutaines, and they imbrace the rock for want of a covering.
24.9: They pluck the fatherles from the breast, and take the pledge of the poor.
24.10: They cause him to go naked without clothing, and take the glening from the hungrie.
24.11: They that make oyle between their walles, and tread their wine presses, suffer thirst.
24.12: Men cry out of the citie, and the soules of the slayne cry out: yet God doth not charge them with follie.
24.13: These are they, that abhorre the light: they know not the wayes thereof, nor continue in the paths thereof.
24.14: The murtherer riseth earely and killeth the poor and the needie: and in the night he is as a theefe.
24.15: The eye also of the adulterer waiteth for the twilight, and sayth, None eye shall see me, and disguiseth his face.
24.16: They digge through houses in the dark, which they marked for themselves in the day: they know not the light.
24.17: But the morning is even to them as the shadow of death: if one know them, they are in the terrours of the shadow of death.
24.18: He is swift upon the waters: their portion shalbe cursed in the earth: he will not behold the way of the vineyardes.
24.19: As the dry ground and heat consume the snow waters, so shall the grave the sinners.
24.20: The pitiful man shall forget him: the worm shall feel his sweetenes: he shalbe no more remembered, and the wicked shalbe broke like a tree.
24.21: He doth evil intreat ye barren, that doeth not bear, neither doeth he good to the widow.
24.22: He draweth also the mighty by his power, and when he riseth up, none is sure of life.
24.23: Though men give him assurance to be in safetie, yet his eyes are upon their wayes.
24.24: They are exalted for a litle, but they are gone, and are brought low as all others: they are destroyed, and cut off as the toppe of an ear of corn.
24.25: But if it be not so, where is he? or who wil prove me a lyer, and make my words of no value?

25.1: Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and sayd,
25.2: Power and fear is with him, that maketh peace in his hie places.
25.3: Is there any nomber in his armies? and upon whom shall not his light arise?
25.4: And how may a man be justified with God? or how can he be clean, that is borne of woman?
25.5: Behold, he wil give no light to the moon, and the starres are vncleane in his sight.
25.6: How much more man, a worm, even the sonne of man, which is but a worm?

26.2: Whom helpest thou? him that hath no power? savest thou the arm that hath no strength?
26.3: Whom counsellest thou? him that hath no wisedome? thou shewest right well as the thing is.
26.4: To whom doest thou declare these words? or whose spirit cometh out of thee?
26.5: The dead things are formed under the waters, and neere unto them.
26.6: The grave is naked before him, and there is no covering for destruction.
26.7: He stretcheth out the North over the emptie place, and hangeth the earth upon nothing.
26.8: He bindeth the waters in his cloudes, and the cloud is not broken under them.
26.9: He holdeth back the face of his throne: and spreadeth his cloud upon it.
26.10: He hath set bounds about the waters, until the day and night come to an end.
26.11: The pillars of heaven tremble and quake at his reproof.
26.12: The sea is calm by his power, and by his understanding he smiteth the pride thereof.
26.13: His Spirit hath garnished the heavens, and his hand hath formed the crooked serpent.
26.14: Loe, these are part of his wayes: but how litle a portion hear we of him? and who can understand his fearefull power?

27.1: Moreover Job proceeded and continued his parable, saying,
27.2: The living God hath taken away my iudgement: for the Almightie hath put my soul in bitterness.
27.3: Yet so long as my breath is in me, and the Spirit of God in my nostrels,
27.4: My lips surely shall speak no wickedness, and my tongue shall utter no deceit.
27.5: God forbid, that I should iustifie you: until I dye, I will never take away mine innocencie from my self.
27.6: I will keep my righteousness, and wil not forsake it: mine heart shall not reprooue me of my dayes.
27.7: Mine enemie shall be as the wicked, and he that riseth against me, as the unrighteous.
27.8: For what hope hath the hypocrite when he hath heaped up riches, if God take away his soul?
27.9: Will God hear his cry, when trouble cometh upon him?
27.10: Will he set his delight on the Almightie? will he call upon God at all times?
27.11: I will teach you what is in the hand of God, and I wil not conceal that which is with the Almightie.
27.12: Behold, all ye your selves have seen it: why then doe you thus vanish in vanitie?
27.13: This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage of tyrants, which they shall receive of the Almightie.
27.14: If his children be in great nomber, the sword shall destroy them, and his posteritie shall not be satisfied with bread.
27.15: His remnant shall be buried in death, and his widowes shall not weep.
27.16: Though he should heap up silver as the dust, and prepare rayment as the clay,
27.17: He may prepare it, but the just shall put it on, and the innocent shall deuide the silver.
27.18: He buildeth his house as the moth, and as a lodge that the watchman maketh.
27.19: When the rich man sleepeth, he shall not be gathered to his fathers: they opened their eyes, and he was gone.
27.20: Terrours shall take him as waters, and a tempest shall cary him away by night.
27.21: The East wind shall take him away, and he shall depart: and it shall hurl him out of his place.
27.22: And God shall cast upon him and not spare, though he would fain flee out of his hand.
27.23: Every man shall clap their hands at him, and hiss at him out of their place.

28.1: The silver surely hath his veyne, and ye gold his place, where they take it.
28.2: Yron is taken out of the dust, and brass is molten out of the stone.
28.3: God putteth an end to darkenesse, and he tryeth the perfection of all things: he setteth a bond of darkenesse, and of the shadow of death.
28.4: The flood breaketh out against the inhabitant, and the waters forgotten of the foot, being higher then man, are gone away.
28.5: Out of the same earth cometh bread, and under it, as it were fire is turned up.
28.6: The stones thereof are a place of saphirs, and the dust of it is gold.
28.7: There is a path which no fowl hath knowen, neyther hath the kites eye seen it.
28.8: The lyons whelpes have not walked it, nor the lyon passed thereby.
28.9: He putteth his hand upon the rockes, and overthroweth the mountaines by the rootes.
28.10: He breaketh rivers in the rockes, and his eye seeth every precious thing.
28.11: He bindeth the floods, that they doe not overflow, and the thing that is hid, bringeth he to light.
28.12: But where is wisdom found? and where is the place of understanding?
28.13: Man knoweth not the price thereof: for it is not found in the land of the living.
28.14: The depth sayth, It is not in mee: the sea also sayth, It is not with me.
28.15: Gold shall not be given for it, neyther shall silver be weighed for the price thereof.
28.16: It shall not be valued with the wedge of gold of Ophir, nor with the precious onix, nor the saphir.
28.17: The gold nor the chrystall shall be equal unto it, nor the exchange shalbe for plate of fine gold.
28.18: No mention shall be made of coral, nor of the gabish: for wisedome is more precious then pearles.
28.19: The Topaz of Ethiopia shall not be equal unto it, neither shall it be valued with the wedge of pure gold.
28.20: Whence then cometh wisedome? and where is the place of understanding,
28.21: Seeing it is hid from the eyes of all the living, and is hid from the foules of the heaven?
28.22: Destruction and death say, We have heard the fame thereof with our eares.
28.23: But God understandeth the way thereof, and he knoweth the place thereof.
28.24: For he beholdeth the endes of the world, and seeth all that is under heaven,
28.25: To make the weight of the windes, and to weigh the waters by measure.
28.26: When he made a decree for the rayne, and a way for the lightening of the thunders,
28.27: Then did he see it, and counted it: he prepared it and also considered it.
28.28: And unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisedome, and to depart from evil is understanding.

29.1: So Job proceeded and continued his parable, saying,
29.2: Oh that I were as in times past, when God preserved me!
29.3: When his light shined upon mine head: and when by his light I walked thorowe the darkenesse,
29.4: As I was in the dayes of my youth: when Gods providence was upon my tabernacle:
29.5: When the almightie was yet with me, and my children round about me.
29.6: When I washed my pathes with butter, and when the rock powred me out rivers of oyle:
29.7: When I went out to the gate, even to the iudgement seat, and when I caused them to prepare my seat in the street.
29.8: The yong men saw me, and hid themselves, and the aged arose, and stood up.
29.9: The princes stayed talk, and layde their hand on their mouth.
29.10: The voyce of princes was hid, and their tongue cleaved to the roof of their mouth.
29.11: And when the ear heard me, it blessed me: and when the eye saw me, it gave witness to me.
29.12: For I delivered the poor that cryed, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him.
29.13: The blessing of him that was ready to perish, came upon me, and I caused the widowes heart to reioyce.
29.14: I put on justice, and it covered me: my iudgement was as a robe, and a crown.
29.15: I was the eyes to the blind, and I was the feet to the lame.
29.16: I was a father unto the poor, and when I knew not the cause, I sought it out diligently.
29.17: I brake also the chawes of the unrighteous man, and pluckt the pray out of his teeth.
29.18: Then I sayde, I shall die in my nest, and I shall multiplie my dayes as the sand.
29.19: For my root is spread out by the water, and the dew shall lye upon my branch.
29.20: My glory shall renue toward me, and my bow shall be restored in mine hand.
29.21: Unto me men gave ear, and wayted, and held their tongue at my counsel.
29.22: After my wordes they replied not, and my talk dropped upon them.
29.23: And they wayted for me, as for the rain, and they opened their mouth as for the latter rayne.
29.24: If I laughed on them, they beleeued it not: neither did they cause the light of my countenance to fall.
29.25: I appoynted out their way, and did sit as chief, and dwelt as a King in the army, and like him that comforteth the mourners.

30.1: But now they that are yonger then I, mock me: yea, they whose fathers I have refused to set with the dogges of my flockes.
30.2: For whereto should the strength of their handes have served mee, seeing age perished in them?
30.3: For pouertie and famine they were solitary, fleeing into the wildernes, which is dark, desolate and waste.
30.4: They cut up nettels by the bushes, and the juniper rootes was their meat.
30.5: They were chased forth from among men: they shouted at them, as at a theefe.
30.6: Therfore they dwelt in the clefts of rivers, in the holes of the earth and rockes.
30.7: They roared among the bushes, and under the thistles they gathered themselves.
30.8: They were the children of fooles and the children of villaines, which were more vile then the earth.
30.9: And now am I their song, and I am their talk.
30.10: They abhorre me, and flee far from mee, and spare not to spit in my face.
30.11: Because that God hath loosed my cord and humbled mee, they have loosed the bridle before me.
30.12: The youth rise up at my right hand: they have pusht my feet, and have trode on me as on the paths of their destruction.
30.13: They have destroyed my paths: they took pleasure at my calamitie, they had none help.
30.14: They came as a great breach of waters, and under this calamitie they come on heapes.
30.15: Fear is turned upon mee: and they pursue my soul as the wind, and mine health passeth away as a cloud.
30.16: Therefore my soul is now powred out upon me, and the dayes of affliction have taken hold on me.
30.17: It pearceth my bones in the night, and my sinewes take no rest.
30.18: For the great vehemencie is my garment changed, which compasseth me about as the colar of my coat.
30.19: He hath cast me into the myre, and I am become like ashes and dust.
30.20: Whe I cry unto thee, thou doest not hear me, neither regardest me, when I stand up.
30.21: Thou turnest thy self cruelly against me, and art enemie unto mee with the strength of thine hand.
30.22: Thou takest me up and causest mee to ride upon the wind, and makest my strength to fail.
30.23: Surely I know that thou wilt bring mee to death, and to the house appoynted for all the living.
30.24: Doubtles none can stretch his hand unto the grave, though they cry in his destruction.
30.25: Did not I weep with him that was in trouble? was not my soul in heaviness for the poor?
30.26: Yet when I looked for good, evil came unto me: and when I waited for light, there came darkenesse.
30.27: My bowels did boyle without rest: for the dayes of affliction are come upon me.
30.28: I went mourning without sunne: I stood up in the congregation and cryed.
30.29: I am a brother to the dragons, and a companion to the ostriches.
30.30: My skinne is black upon me, and my bones are burnt with heat.
30.31: Therefore mine harp is turned to mourning, and mine organs into the voyce of them that weep.

31.1: I made a covenant with mine eyes: why then should I think on a mayde?
31.2: For what portion should I have of God from above? and what inheritance of the Almightie from on hie?
31.3: Is not destruction to the wicked and strange punishment to the workers of iniquitie?
31.4: Doeth not he behold my wayes and tell all my steps?
31.5: If I have walked in vanitie, or if my foot hath made haste to deceit,
31.6: Let God weigh me in the just balance, and he shall know mine vprightnes.
31.7: If my steppe hath turned out of the way, or mine heart hath walked after mine eye, or if any blot hath cleaved to mine handes,
31.8: Let me sow, and let another eat: yea, let my plantes be rooted out.
31.9: If mine heart hath been deceived by a woman, or if I have layde wayte at the door of my neighbour,
31.10: Let my wife grind unto another man, and let other men bow down upon her:
31.11: For this is a wickednes, and iniquitie to bee condemned:
31.12: Yea, this is a fire that shall deuoure to destruction, and which shall root out al mine increase,
31.13: If I did contemn the iudgement of my servant, and of my mayde, when they did contend with me,
31.14: What then shall I do when God standeth up? and when he shall visit me, what shall I answer?
31.15: He that hath made me in the womb, hath he not made him? hath not he alone facioned us in the womb?
31.16: If I restrained the poor of their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail,
31.17: Or have eaten my morsels alone, and the fatherles hath not eaten thereof,
31.18: (For from my youth hee hath growen up with me as with a father, and from my mothers womb I have been a guide unto her)
31.19: If I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or any poor without covering,
31.20: If his loynes have not blessed me, because he was warmed with the fleece of my sheep,
31.21: If I have lift up mine hand against the fatherless, when I saw that I might help him in the gate,
31.22: Let mine arm fal from my shoulder, and mine arm be broken from the bone.
31.23: For Gods punishment was fearefull unto me, and I could not be delivered from his highnes.
31.24: If I made gold mine hope, or have sayd to the wedge of gold, Thou art my confidence,
31.25: If I reioyced because my substance was great, or because mine hand had gotten much,
31.26: If I did behold the sunne, when it shined, or the moon, walking in her brightnes,
31.27: If mine heart did flatter me in secret, or if my mouth did kiss mine hand,
31.28: (This also had been an iniquitie to be condemned: for I had denied the God above)
31.29: If I reioyced at his destruction that hated me, or was mooued to ioye when evil came upon him,
31.30: Neither have I suffred my mouth to sinne, by wishing a curse unto his soul.
31.31: Did not the men of my Tabernacle say, Who shall give us of his flesh? we can not bee satisfied.
31.32: The stranger did not lodge in the street, but I opened my doores unto him, that went by the way.
31.33: If I have hid my sinne, as Adam, concealing mine iniquitie in my bosom,
31.34: Though I could have made afraid a great multitude, yet the most contemptible of the families did fear me: so I kept silence, and went not out of the door.
31.35: Oh that I had some to hear me! behold my sign that the Almightie will witness for me: though mine adversary should write a book against me,
31.36: Would not I take it upon my shoulder, and bind it as a crown unto me?
31.37: I will tell him the nomber of my goings, and goe unto him as to a prince.
31.38: If my land cry against me, or the furrowes thereof complayne together,
31.39: If I have eaten the fruites thereof without silver: or if I have grieved the soules of the masters thereof,
31.40: Let thistles grow in stead of wheat, and cockle in the stead of Barley. The wordes of Job are ended.

32.1: So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he esteemed himself just.
32.2: Then the wrath of Elihu the sonne of Barachel the Buzite, of the familie of Ram, was kindled: his wrath, I say, was kindled against Job, because he justified himself more then God.
32.3: Also his anger was kindled against his three friends, because they could not find an answer, and yet condemned Job.
32.4: (Now Elihu had wayted til Job had spoken: for they were more ancient in yeeres then he)
32.5: So when Elihu saw, that there was none answer in the mouth of the three men, his wrath was kindled.
32.6: Therefore Elihu the sonne of Barachel, the Buzite answered, and sayd, I am yong in yeres, and ye are ancient: therefore I doubted, and was afraid to shew you mine opinion.
32.7: For I said, The dayes shall speak, and the multitude of yeeres shall teach wisedome.
32.8: Surely there is a spirit in man, but the inspiration of the Almightie giveth understanding.
32.9: Great men are not alway wise, neither doe the aged alway understand iudgement.
32.10: Therefore I say, Hear me, and I will shew also mine opinion.
32.11: Behold, I did wait upon your wordes, and hearkened unto your knowledge, whiles you sought out reasons.
32.12: Yea, when I had considered you, lo, there was none of you that reproved Job, nor answered his wordes:
32.13: Lest ye should say, We have found wisedome: for God hath cast him down, and no man.
32.14: Yet hath he not directed his words to me, neyther will I answer him by your wordes.
32.15: Then they fearing, answered no more, but left off their talk.
32.16: When I had wayted (for they spake not, but stood still and answered no more)
32.17: Then answered I in my turn, and I shewed mine opinion.
32.18: For I am full of matter, and the spirit within me compelleth me.
32.19: Behold, my belly is as the wine, which hath no vent, and like the new bottels that brast.
32.20: Therefore will I speak, that I may take breath: I will open my lippes, and will answer.
32.21: I will not now accept the person of man, neyther will I give titles to man.
32.22: For I may not give titles, lest my Maker should take me away suddenly.

33.1: Wherefore, Job, I pray thee, hear my talk and hearken unto all my wordes.
33.2: Behold now, I have opened my mouth: my tongue hath spoken in my mouth.
33.3: My words are in the vprightnesse of mine heart, and my lippes shall speak pure knowledge.
33.4: The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almightie hath given me life.
33.5: If thou canst give me answer, prepare thy self and stand before me.
33.6: Behold, I am according to thy wish in Gods stead: I am also formed of the clay.
33.7: Behold, my terrour shall not fear thee, neither shall mine hand be heauie upon thee.
33.8: Doubtles thou hast spoken in mine eares, and I have heard the voyce of thy wordes.
33.9: I am clean, without sinne: I am innocent, and there is none iniquitie in me.
33.10: Lo, he hath found occasions against me, and counted me for his enemie.
33.11: He hath put my feet in the stockes, and looketh narrowly unto all my paths.
33.12: Behold, in this hast thou not done right: I will answer thee, that God is greater then man.
33.13: Why doest thou strive against him? for he doeth not give account of all his matters.
33.14: For God speaketh once or twise, and one seeth it not.
33.15: In dreames and visions of the night, when sleep falleth upon men, and they sleep upon their beds,
33.16: Then he openeth the eares of men, even by their corrections, which he had sealed,
33.17: That he might cause man to turn away from his enterprise, and that he might hide the pride of man,
33.18: And keep back his soul from the pit, and that his life should not pass by the sword.
33.19: He is also striken with sorow upon his bed, and the grief of his bones is sore,
33.20: So that his life causeth him to abhorre bread, and his soul daintie meat.
33.21: His flesh faileth that it can not be seen, and his bones which were not seen, clatter.
33.22: So his soul draweth to the grave, and his life to the buriers.
33.23: If there be a messenger with him, or an interpreter, one of a thousand to declare unto man his righteousness,
33.24: Then will he have mercie upon him, and will say, Deliver him, that he go not down into the pit: for I have received a reconciliation.
33.25: Then shall his flesh be as fresh as a childes, and shall return as in the dayes of his youth.
33.26: He shall pray unto God, and he will be fauourable unto him, and he shall see his face with joy: for he will render unto man his righteousnes.
33.27: He looketh upon men, and if one say, I have sinned, and perverted righteousness, and it did not profit me,
33.28: He will deliver his soul from going into the pit, and his life shall see the light.
33.29: Lo, all these things will God work twise or thrise with a man,
33.30: That he may turn back his soul from the pit, to be illuminate in the light of the living.
33.31: Mark well, O Job, and hear me: keep silence, and I will speak.
33.32: If there be matter, answer me, and speak: for I desire to iustifie thee.
33.33: If thou hast not, hear me: hold thy tongue, and I will teach thee wisedome.

34.2: Hear my wordes, ye wise men, and hearken unto me, ye that have knowledge.
34.3: For the ear tryeth the words, as the mouth tasteth meat.
34.4: Let us seek iudgement among us, and let us know among our selves what is good.
34.5: For Job hath said, I am righteous, and God hath taken away my iudgement.
34.6: Should I lye in my right? my wound of the arrow is grieuous without my sinne.
34.7: What man is like Job, that drinketh scornfulnesse like water?
34.8: Which goeth in the companie of them that work iniquitie, and walketh with wicked men?
34.9: For he hath said, It profiteth a man nothing that he should walk with God.
34.10: Therefore hearken unto me, ye men of wisedome, God forbid that wickedness should be in God, and iniquitie in the Almightie.
34.11: For he will render unto man according to his work, and cause every one to find according to his way.
34.12: And certainely God will not do wickedly, neither will the Almightie pervert iudgement.
34.13: Whom hath he appointed over the earth beside him self? or who hath placed the whole world?
34.14: If he set his heart upon man, and gather unto him self his spirit and his breath,
34.15: All flesh shall perish together, and man shall return unto dust.
34.16: And if thou hast understanding, hear this and hearken to the voyce of my wordes.
34.17: Shal he that hateth iudgement, govern? and wilt thou judge him wicked that is most just?
34.18: Wilt thou say unto a King, Thou art wicked? or to princes, Ye are ungodly?
34.19: How much less to him that accepteth not the persons of princes, and regardeth not the rich, more then the poor? for they be all the work of his handes.
34.20: They shall die suddenly, and the people shalbe troubled at midnight, and they shall pass foorth and take away the mightie without hand.
34.21: For his eyes are upon the wayes of man, and he seeth all his goings.
34.22: There is no darkenesse nor shadow of death, that the workers of iniquitie might be hid therein.
