34.23: For he will not lay on man so much, that he should enter into iudgement with God.
34.24: He shall break the mightie without seeking, and shall set up other in their stead.
34.25: Therefore shall he declare their works: he shall turn the night, and they shalbe destroyed.
34.26: He striketh them as wicked men in the places of the seers,
34.27: Because they have turned back from him, and would not consider all his wayes:
34.28: So that they have caused the voyce of the poor to come unto him, and he hath heard the cry of the afflicted.
34.29: And when he giveth quietness, who can make trouble? and when he hideth his face, who can behold him, whether it be upon nations, or upon a man onely?
34.30: Because the hypocrite doeth reign, and because the people are snared.
34.31: Surely it appertaineth unto God to say, I have pardoned, I will not destroy.
34.32: But if I see not, teach thou me: if I have done wickedly, I will doe no more.
34.33: Wil he perform the thing through thee? for thou hast reproved it, because that thou hast chosen, and not I. now speak what thou knowest.
34.34: Let men of understanding tell me, and let a wise man hearken unto me.
34.35: Job hath not spoken of knowledge, neyther were his wordes according to wisedome.
34.36: I desire that Job may be tryed, unto the end touching the answeres for wicked men.
34.37: For he addeth rebellion unto his sinne: he clappeth his handes among us, and multiplieth his wordes against God.

35.2: Thinkest thou this right, that thou hast said, I am more righteous then God?
35.3: For thou hast said, What profiteth it thee and what availeth it me, to purge me from my sinne?
35.4: Therefore will I answer thee, and thy companions with thee.
35.5: Look unto the heaven, and see and behold the cloudes which are hyer then thou.
35.6: If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him, yea, when thy sinnes be many, what doest thou unto him?
35.7: If thou be righteous, what givest thou unto him? or what receiveth he at thine hand?
35.8: Thy wickedness may hurt a man as thou art: and thy righteousnes may profit ye sonne of man.
35.9: They cause many that are oppressed, to cry, which cry out for ye violence of the mightie.
35.10: But none saieth, Where is God that made me, which giveth songs in the nyght?
35.11: Which teacheth us more then the beastes of the earth, and giveth us more wisdom then the foules of the heaven.
35.12: Then they cry because of the violence of the wicked, but he answereth not.
35.13: Surely God will not hear vanitie, neyther will the Almightie regard it.
35.14: Although thou sayest to God, Thou wilt not regard it, yet iudgement is before him: trust thou in him.
35.15: But now because his anger hath not visited, nor called to count the evil with great extremitie,
35.16: Therfore Job openeth his mouth in vain, and multiplieth wordes without knowledge.

36.2: Suffer me a litle, and I will instruct thee: for I have yet to speak on Gods behalf.
36.3: I will fetch my knowledge afarre off, and will attribute righteousnes unto my Maker.
36.4: For truely my wordes shall not be false, and he that is perfect in knowledge, speaketh with thee.
36.5: Behold, the mighty God casteth away none that is mighty and valiant of courage.
36.6: He mainteineth not the wicked, but he giveth iudgement to the afflicted.
36.7: He withdraweth not his eyes from the righteous, but they are with Kings in ye throne, where he placeth them for ever: thus they are exalted.
36.8: And if they bee bound in fetters and tyed with the cordes of affliction,
36.9: Then will he shew them their work and their sinnes, because they have been proud.
36.10: He openeth also their ear to discipline, and commandeth them that they return from iniquity.
36.11: If they obey and serve him, they shall end their dayes in prosperity, and their yeres in pleasures.
36.12: But if they wil not obey, they shall pass by the sword, and perish without knowledge.
36.13: But the hypocrites of heart increase the wrath: for they call not when he bindeth them.
36.14: Their soul dyeth in youth, and their life among the whoremongers.
36.15: He delivereth the poor in his affliction, and openeth their ear in trouble.
36.16: Even so would he have taken thee out of the streight place into a broad place and not shut up beneath: and that which resteth upon thy table, had been full of fat.
36.17: But thou art ful of the iudgement of the wicked, though iudgement and equitie maintain all things.
36.18: For Gods wrath is, least hee should take that away in thine abundance: for no multitude of giftes can deliver thee.
36.19: Wil he regard thy riches? he regardeth not gold, nor all them that excel in strength.
36.20: Be not careful in the night, how he destroyeth the people out of their place.
36.21: Take thou heed: look not to iniquitie: for thou hast chosen it rather then affliction.
36.22: Behold, God exalteth by his power: what teacher is like him?
36.23: Who hath appointed to him his way? or who can say, Thou hast done wickedly?
36.24: Remember that thou magnifie his work, which men behold.
36.25: All men see it, and men behold it afarre off.
36.26: Behold, God is excellent, and we know him not, neither can the nomber of his yeres bee searched out.
36.27: When he restraineth the droppes of water, the rayne powreth down by the vapour thereof,
36.28: Which rain the cloudes do droppe and let fall abundantly upon man.
36.29: Who can know the divisions of ye clouds and the thunders of his tabernacle?
36.30: Behold, he spreadeth his light upon it, and covereth the bottom of the sea.
36.31: For thereby hee judgeth the people, and giveth meat abundantly.
36.32: He covereth the light with the clouds, and commandeth them to go against it.
36.33: His companion sheweth him thereof, and there is anger in rising up.

37.1: At this also mine heart is astonied, and is mooued out of his place.
37.2: Hear the sound of his voyce, and the noyse that goeth out of his mouth.
37.3: He directeth it under the whole heaven, and his light unto the endes of the world.
37.4: After it a noyse soundeth: hee thundereth with the voyce of his maiestie, and hee will not stay them when his voyce is heard.
37.5: God thundereth marueilously with his voyce: he worketh great things, which we know not.
37.6: For he sayth to the snow, Be thou upon the earth: likewise to the small rayne and to the great rayne of his power.
37.7: With the force thereof he shutteth up every man, that all men may know his work.
37.8: Then the beastes go into the denne, and remain in their places.
37.9: The whirlewind cometh out of the South, and the cold from the North wind.
37.10: At the breath of God the frost is given, and the breadth of the waters is made narrow.
37.11: He maketh also the cloudes to labour, to water the earth, and scattereth the cloud of his light.
37.12: And it is turned about by his government, that they may doe whatsoever he commandeth them upon the whole world:
37.13: Whether it be for punishment, or for his land, or of mercie, he causeth it to come.
37.14: Hearken unto this, O Job: stand and consider the wonderous workes of God.
37.15: Diddest thou know when God disposed them? and caused the light of his cloud to shine?
37.16: Hast thou knowen the varietie of the cloud, and the wonderous workes of him, that is perfite in knowledge?
37.17: Or how thy clothes are warm, when he maketh the earth quiet through the South wind?
37.18: Hast thou stretched out the heaues, which are strong, and as a molten glass?
37.19: Tell us what we shall say unto him: for we can not dispose our matter because of darknes.
37.20: Shall it be told him when I speak? or shall man speak when he shalbe destroyed?
37.21: And now men see not the light, which shineth in the cloudes, but the wind passeth and clenseth them.
37.22: The brightness cometh out of the North: the praise thereof is to God, which is terrible.
37.23: It is the Almightie: we can not find him out: he is excellent in power and iudgement, and aboundant in justice: he afflicteth not.
37.24: Let men therefore fear him: for he will not regard any that are wise in their own conceit.

38.1: Then answered the Lord unto Job out of the whirle wind, and said,
38.2: Who is this that darkeneth the counsel by wordes without knowledge?
38.3: Gird up now thy loynes like a man: I will demand of thee and declare thou unto me.
38.4: Where wast thou when I layd the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding,
38.5: Who hath layde the measures thereof, if thou knowest, or who hath stretched the line over it:
38.6: Whereupon are the foundations thereof set: or who layed the corner stone thereof:
38.7: When the starres of the morning praysed me together, and all the children of God reioyced:
38.8: Or who hath shut up the Sea with doores, when it yssued and came foorth as out of the womb:
38.9: When I made the cloudes as a covering thereof, and darkenesse as the swadeling bands thereof:
38.10: When I stablished my commandement upon it, and set barres and doores,
38.11: And said, Hitherto shalt thou come, but no farther, and here shall it stay thy proud waves.
38.12: Hast thou commanded the morning since thy dayes? hast thou caused the morning to know his place,
38.13: That it might take hold of the corners of the earth, and that the wicked might be shaken out of it?
38.14: It is turned as clay to facion, and all stand up as a garment.
38.15: And from the wicked their light shall be taken away, and the hie arm shalbe broken.
38.16: Hast thou entred into the bottomes of the sea? or hast thou walked to seek out the depth?
38.17: Have the gates of death been opened unto thee? or hast thou seen the gates of the shadow of death?
38.18: Hast thou perceived the breadth of the earth? tell if thou knowest all this.
38.19: Where is the way where light dwelleth? and where is the place of darkenesse,
38.20: That thou shouldest receive it in the boundes thereof, and that thou shouldest know the paths to the house thereof?
38.21: Knewest thou it, because thou wast then borne, and because the nomber of thy dayes is great?
38.22: Hast thou entred into the treasures of the snow? or hast thou seen the treasures of ye hail,
38.23: Which I have hid against the time of trouble, against the day of war and battell?
38.24: By what way is the light parted, which scattereth the East wind upon the earth?
38.25: Who hath deuided the spowtes for the rain? or the way for the lightning of ye thunders,
38.26: To cause it to rain on the earth where no man is, and in the wildernes where there is no man?
38.27: To fulfil the wild and waste place, and to cause the bud of the herb to spring forth?
38.28: Who is the father of the rayne? or who hath begotten the droppes of the dew?
38.29: Out of whose womb came the yee? who hath ingendred the frost of the heaven?
38.30: The waters are hid as with a stone: and the face of the depth is frosen.
38.31: Canst thou restrain the sweet influences of the Pleiades? or loose the bandes of Orion?
38.32: Canst thou bring foorth Mazzaroth in their time? canst thou also guide Arcturus with his sonnes?
38.33: Knowest thou the course of heaven, or canst thou set the rule thereof in the earth?
38.34: Canst thou lift up thy voice to the cloudes that the aboundance of water may cover thee?
38.35: Canst thou send the lightenings that they may walk, and say unto thee, Loe, heere we are?
38.36: Who hath put wisedome in the reines? or who hath given the heart understanding?
38.37: Who can nomber cloudes by wisedome? or who can cause to cease the bottels of heave,
38.38: When the earth groweth into hardness, and the clottes are fast together?

39.1: Wilt thou hunt the pray for the lyon? or fill the appetite of the lyons whelpes,
39.2: When they couch in their places, and remain in the covert to lye in wait?
39.3: Who prepareth for the raven his meat, when his birdes crie unto God, wandering for lack of meat?
39.4: Knowest thou the time when the wild goates bring foorth yong? or doest thou mark when the hindes doe calve?
39.5: Canst thou nomber the moneths that they fulfil? or knowest thou the time when they bring foorth?
39.6: They bow them selves: they bruise their yong and cast out their sorowes.
39.7: Yet their yong wax fatte, and grow up with corn: they goe foorth and return not unto them.
39.8: Who hath set the wild ass at libertie? or who hath loosed the bondes of the wild ass?
39.9: It is I which have made the wilderness his house, and the salt places his dwellings.
39.10: He derideth the multitude of the citie: he heareth not the crie of the driver.
39.11: He seeketh out the mountain for his pasture, and searcheth after every green thing.
39.12: Will the vnicorne serve thee? or will he tary by thy cribbe?
39.13: Canst thou bind the vnicorne with his band to labour in the furrow? or will he plow the valleyes after thee?
39.14: Wilt thou trust in him, because his strength is great, and cast off thy labour unto him?
39.15: Wilt thou beleeue him, that he will bring home thy seed, and gather it unto thy barn?
39.16: Hast thou given the pleasant wings unto the peacockes? or winges and feathers unto the ostrich?
39.17: Which leaveth his egges in the earth, and maketh them hot in the dust,
39.18: And forgetteth that the foot might scatter the, or that the wild beast might break the.
39.19: He sheweth himself cruel unto his yong ones, as they were not his, and is without fear, as if he travailed in vain.
39.20: For God had deprived him of wisedom, and hath given him no part of understanding.
39.21: When time is, he mounteth on hie: he mocketh the horse and his rider.
39.22: Hast thou given the horse strength? or covered his neck with neying?
39.23: Hast thou made him afraid as the grashopper? his strong neying is fearefull.
39.24: He diggeth in the valley, and reioyceth in his strength: he goeth foorth to meet the harnest man.
39.25: He mocketh at fear, and is not afraid, and turneth not back from the sword,
39.26: Though the quiuer rattle against him, the glittering spear and the shield.
39.27: He swalloweth the ground for fearcenes and rage, and he beleeueth not that it is the noise of the trumpet.
39.28: He sayth among the trumpets, Ha, ha: hee smelleth the battell afarre off, and the noyse of the captaines, and the shouting.
39.29: Shall the hauke flie by thy wisedome, stretching out his wings toward the South?
39.30: Doeth the eagle mount up at thy commandement, or make his nest on hie?
39.31: She abideth and remaineth in the rock, even upon the toppe of the rock, and the tower.
39.32: From thence she spieth for meat, and her eyes behold afarre off.
39.33: His young ones also suck up blood: and where the slain are, there is she.
39.34: Moreover ye Lord spake unto Job, and said,
39.35: Is this to learn to strive with the Almightie? he that reprooueth God, let him answer to it.
39.36: Then Job answered the Lord, saying,
39.37: Behold, I am vile: what shall I answer thee? I will lay mine hand upon my mouth.
39.38: Once have I spoken, but I will answer no more, yea twise, but I will proceed no further.

40.1: Again the Lord answered Job out of the whirle wind, and said,
40.2: Gird up now thy loynes like a man: I will demaunde of thee, and declare thou unto me.
40.3: Wilt thou disanul my iudgement? or wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayst be justified?
40.4: Or hast thou an arm like God? or doest thou thunder with a voyce like him?
40.5: Deck thy self now with maiestie and excellencie, and aray thy self with beautie and glory.
40.6: Cast abroad the indignation of thy wrath, and behold every one that is proud, and abase him.
40.7: Look on every one that is arrogant, and bring him low: and destroy the wicked in their place.
40.8: Hide them in the dust together, and bind their faces in a secret place.
40.9: Then will I confess unto thee also, that thy right hand can save thee.
40.10: Behold now Behemoth (whom I made with thee) which eateth grass as an oxe.
40.11: Behold now, his strength is in his loynes, and his force is in the nauil of his belly.
40.12: When hee taketh pleasure, his tail is like a cedar: the sinews of his stones are wrapt together.
40.13: His bones are like staves of brass, and his small bones like staves of yron.
40.14: He is the chief of the wayes of God: he that made him, will make his sword to approch unto him.
40.15: Surely the mountaines bring him foorth grass, where all the beastes of the field play.
40.16: Lyeth hee under the trees in the covert of the reed and fennes?
40.17: Can the trees cover him with their shadow? or can the willowes of the river compass him about?
40.18: Behold, he spoyleth the river, and hasteth not: he trusteth that he can draw up Iorden into his mouth.
40.19: Hee taketh it with his eyes, and thrusteth his nose through whatsoever meeteth him.
40.20: Canst thou draw out Liuiathan with an hook, and with a line which thou shalt cast down unto his tongue?
40.21: Canst thou cast an hook into his nose? canst thou perce his iawes with an angle?
40.22: Will he make many prayers unto thee, or speak thee fair?
40.23: Will hee make a covenant with thee? and wilt thou take him as a servant for ever?
40.24: Wilt thou play with him as with a bird? or wilt thou bynd him for thy maydes?
40.25: Shall the companions baket with him? shall they deuide him among the marchants?
40.26: Canst thou fill the basket with his skinne? or the fishpanier with his head?
40.27: Lay thine hand upon him: remember the battel, and do no more so.
40.28: Behold, his hope is in vain: for shall not one perish even at the sight of him?

41.1: None is so fearce that dare stirre him up. Who is he then that can stand before me?
41.2: Who hath prevented mee that I should make an end? Al under heaven is mine.
41.3: I will not keep silence concerning his partes, nor his power nor his comely proportion.
41.4: Who can discover the face of his garmet? or who shall come to him with a double bridle?
41.5: Who shall open the doores of his face? his teeth are fearefull round about.
41.6: The maiestie of his scales is like strog shields, and are sure sealed.
41.7: One is set to another, that no wind can come between them.
41.8: One is ioyned to another: they stick together, that they cannot be sundered.
41.9: His niesings make the light to shine, and his eyes are like the eyelids of the morning.
41.10: Out of his mouth go lampes, and sparkes of fire leap out.
41.11: Out of his nostrels cometh out smoke, as out of a boyling pot or caldron.
41.12: His breath maketh the coales burn: for a flame goeth out of his mouth.
41.13: In his neck remayneth strength, and labour is reiected before his face.
41.14: The members of his bodie are ioyned: they are strong in themselves, and cannot be mooued.
41.15: His heart is as strong as a stone, and as hard as the nether milstone.
41.16: The mightie are afrayd of his maiestie, and for fear they faint in themselves.
41.17: When the sword doeth touch him, he will not rise up, nor for the spear, dart nor habergeon.
41.18: He esteemeth yron as straw, and brass as rotten wood.
41.19: The archer canot make him flee: ye stones of the sling are turned into stubble unto him:
41.20: The dartes are counted as straw: and hee laugheth at the shaking of the spear.
41.21: Sharp stones are under him, and he spreadeth sharp things upon the myre.
41.22: He maketh the depth to boyle like a pot, and maketh the sea like a pot of oyntment.
41.23: He maketh a path to shine after him: one would think the depth as an hoar head.
41.24: In the earth there is none like him: hee is made without fear.
41.25: He beholdeth al hie things: he is a King over all the children of pride.

42.1: Then Job answered the Lord, and sayd,
42.2: I know that thou canst doe all things, and that there is no thought hid from thee.
42.3: Who is hee that hideth counsel without knowledge? therefore have I spoken that I understood not, even things too wonderful for me, and which I knew not.
42.4: Hear, I beseech thee, and I will speak: I will demaunde of thee, and declare thou unto me.
42.5: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear, but now mine eye seeth thee.
42.6: Therefore I abhorre my self, and repent in dust and ashes.
42.7: Now after that the Lord had spoken these wordes unto Job, ye Lord also said unto Eliphaz ye Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for yee have not spoken of me the thing that is right, like my servant Job.
42.8: Therefore take unto you now seven bullockes, and seven rammes, and go to my servant Job, and offer up for your selves a burnt offring, and my servant Job shall pray for you: for I wil accept him, least I should put you to shame, because ye have not spoken of me the thing, which is right, like my servant Job.
42.9: So Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went, and did according as the Lord had said unto them, and the Lord accepted Job.
42.10: Then the Lord turned the captiuitie of Job, when he prayed for his friends: also the Lord gave Job twise so much as he had before.
42.11: Then came unto him all his brethren, and all his sisters, and all they that had been of his acquaintance before, and did eat bread with him in his house, and had compassion of him, and comforted him for al the evil, that the Lord had brought upon him, and every man gave him a piece of money, and every one an earing of gold.
42.12: So the Lord blessed the last dayes of Job more then the first: for he had foureteene thousand sheep, and six thousand camels, and a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she asses.
42.13: He had also seue sonnes, and three daughters.
42.14: And he called the name of one Iemimah, and the name of the second Keziah, and the name of the third Keren-happuch.
42.15: In all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of Job, and their father gave them inheritaunce among their brethren.
42.16: And after this lived Job an hundreth and fourtie yeres, and saw his sonnes, and his sonnes sonnes, even four generations.
42.17: So Job dyed, being old, and full of dayes.

18:1:1: That is, of the country of Idumea, as Lam. 4:21, or bordering thereupon: for the land was called by the name of Uz, the son of Dishan the son of Seir, Gen. 36:28.
Forasmuch as he was a Gentile, and not a Jew, and yet is pronounced upright, and without hypocrisy, it declareth that among the heathen God hath his.
Hereby is declared, what is meant by an upright and just man.
18:1:3: His children and riches are declared, to commend his virtue in his prosperity and his patience, and constancy, when God had taken them from him.
Meaning, the Arabians, Chaldeans, Idumeans, etc.
18:1:5: That is, commanded them to be sanctified: meaning, that they should consider the faults that they had committed, and reconcile themselves for the same.
That is, he offered for every one of his children an offering of reconciliation, which declared his religion toward God, and the care that he had toward his children.
In Hebrew it is, and blessed God, which is sometimes taken for blaspheming and cursing, as here and 1 Kings 21:10, 13, etc.
18:1:6: Meaning, the Angels, which are called the sons of God, because they are willing to execute his will.
Because our infirmity cannot comprehend God in his majesty, he is set forth unto us as a King, that our capacity may be able to understand that which is spoken of him.
This declareth, that although Satan be adversary to God, yet he is compelled to obey him, and do him all homage, without whose permission and appointment he can do nothing.
18:1:7: This question is asked for our infirmity: for God knew whence he came.
Herein is described the nature of Satan, which is ever ranging for his prey, 1 Pet. 5:8.
18:1:9: He feareth thee not for thine own sake, but for the commodity that he received by thee.
18:1:10: Meaning, the grace of God, which served Job as a rampart against all tentations.
18:1:11: This signifieth, that Satan is not able to touch us, but it is God that must do it.

Satan noteth the vice whereunto men are commonly subject, that is, to hide their rebellion, and to be content with God in the time of prosperity, which view is disclosed in the time of their adversity.
18:1:12: That is, went to execute that which God had permitted him to do: for else he can never go out of God’s presence.
God giveth not Satan power over man to gratify him, but to declare that he hath no power over man, but that which God giveth him.
18:1:16: Which thing was also done by the craft of Satan, to tempt Job the more grievously, forasmuch as he might see, that not only men were his enemies, but that God made war against him.
18:1:18: This last plague declareth, that when one plague is past which seemeth hard to be borne, God can send us another far more grievous, to try his, and teach them obedience.
18:1:20: Which came not of impatience, but declareth that the children of God are not insensible like blocks, but that in their patience they feel affliction and grief of mind: yet they keep a mean herein, and rebel not against God, as the wicked do.
18:1:21: That is, into the belly of the earth, which is the mother of all.
Hereby he confesseth that God is just, and good, although his hand be sore upon him.
18:1:22: But declared that God did all things according to justice and equity.
18:2:1: That is, the Angels, as Job 1:6.
18:2:3: That is, when thou hadst nought against him, or when thou wast not able to bring thy purpose to pass.
He proveth Job’s integrity by this that he ceased not to fear God when his plagues were grievously upon him.
18:2:4: Hereby he meant, that a man’s own skin is dearer unto him than another man’s.
18:2:6: Thus Satan can go no further in punishing, than God hath limited him.
18:2:7: This sore was most vehement, wherewith also God plagued the Egyptians, Exod. 9:9, and threateneth to punish the rebellious people, Deut. 28:27, so that this tentation was most grievous: for if Job had measured God’s favor by the vehemency of his disease, he might have thought that God had cast him off.
18:2:8: As destitute of all other help and means, and wonderfully afflicted with the sorrow of his disease.
18:2:9: Satan useth the same instrument against Job, as he did against Adam.

Meaning, what gainest thou to serve God, seeing he thus plagueth thee, as though he were thine enemy? This is the most grievous temptation of the faithful, when their faith is assailed, and when Satan goeth about to persuade them that they trust in God in vain.
For death was appointed to the blasphemer, and so she meant that he should soon be rid out of his pain.
18:2:10: He so bridled his affections, that his tongue through impatience did not murmur against God.
That is, to be patient in adversity, as we rejoice when he sendeth prosperity, and so to acknowledge him to be both merciful and just.
18:2:11: Which were men of authority, wise and learned, and as the Septuagint writes, Kings, and came to comfort him, but when they saw how he was visited, they conceived an evil opinion of him, as though he had been but an hypocrite, and so justly plagued of God for his sins.
18:2:12: This was also a ceremony, which they used in those countries, as the renting of their clothes in sign of sorrow, etc.
18:2:13: And therefore thought that he would not have hearkened unto their counsel.
18:3:1: Here Job beginneth to feel his great imperfection in this battle between the spirit and the flesh, Rom. 7:18, and after a manner yieldeth, yet in the end he getteth victory, though he was in the mean time greatly wounded.
18:3:3: Men ought not to be weary of their life, and curse it, because of the infirmities that it is subject unto, but because they are given to sin and rebellion against God.
18:3:4: Let it be put out of the number of days, and let it not have the light of the Sun to separate it from the night.
18:3:5: That is, most obscure darkness, which maketh them afraid of death that are in it.
18:3:8: Which curse the day of their birth, let them lay that curse upon this night.
18:3:9: Hebrew, The eyelids of the morning.
Let it be always night, and never see day.
18:3:11: This, and that which followeth, declareth, that when man giveth place to his passions, he is not able to stay nor keep measure, but runneth headlong into all evil, except God call him back.
18:3:13: The vehemency of his afflictions made him to utter these words, as though death were the end of all miseries, and as if there were no life after this, which he speaketh not as though it were so, but the infirmities of his flesh caused him to burst out in this error of the wicked.
18:3:14: He noteth the ambition of them, which for their pleasure as it were change the order of nature, and build in most barren places, because they would hereby make their names immortal.
18:3:17: That is, by death the cruelty of the tyrants hath ceased.
18:3:18: All they that sustain any kind of calamity and misery in this world: which he speaketh after the judgment of the flesh.
